extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; educators, school reformers, and social critics
extracted.subtask_short: critique of modern education and schools
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical and prescriptive critique of early-20th-century English education and public schools, arguing what schools should teach, what they currently fail at, and how they should relate to mass culture and moral formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore simplicity rather than suggest complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The real object of our schools should be not so much to suggest complexity as solely to restore simplicity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues schools should counter the over-complication taught by popular culture; instead of adding more abstract expansion, schools should reintroduce clear simple first principles. He warns that the poor are already 'over-educated' by street knowledge and that schools should aim to recover simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools must out‑shine surrounding culture in clarity, kindness, cleverness and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: "A modern London school ought not merely to be clearer, kindlier, more clever and more rapid than ignorance and darkness. It must also be clearer than a picture postcard, cleverer than a Limerick competition, quicker than the tram, and kindlier than the tavern."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The school must provide a superior rival to the constant appeals of advertising, newspapers, trams and taverns; practical examples Chesterton gives include posters, Daily Mail maps, trams, Prizy Bits prizes and tavern culture that teach children the wrong lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture and education require selection and rejection (narrowness/orthodoxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true task of culture to-day is not a task of expansion, but very decidedly of selection--and rejection. The educationist must find a creed and teach it... it must be orthodox."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than vague, all-embracing curricula, educators must choose between competing worldviews (e.g., Kipling vs. Shaw, Harmsworth vs. Pearson) and teach a coherent, fastidious set of convictions; Chesterton frames this as a practical, even 'sectarian', necessity for effective education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical sectarianism in upbringing (decide which influences to endorse)
rubrics_metrics.description: "education must now be sectarian education, merely for practical purposes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton emphasizes that parents and educators inevitably choose whom a child is 'brought up by' (vicar, minister, or particular press/author). The guidance is to accept that choice and make it deliberate and explicit rather than pretend to neutral breadth that yields nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize there are no uneducated people—correct miseducation rather than assume absence
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are no uneducated people. Everybody in England is educated; only most people are educated wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The working poor are already culturally literate in many ways (politics via police news, maps via newspapers); schools must address this existing, often distorted, education ('learn everything tail foremost') and aim to replace bad instruction, not simply supply missing instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools must actively resist and rival mass commercial and political influences
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the newspapers, all the new advertisements, all the new medicines and new theologies, all the glare and blare of the gas and brass of modern times--it is against these that the national school must bear up if it can."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton lists concrete sources (hoardings/advertisements, party newspapers, posters, trams, taverns) and instructs that schools must offer clearer, more humane, and more authoritative alternatives so children are not simply informed by sensational or utilitarian mass culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach a 'philosophy of colors'—contextualize and dignify aesthetic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not colors he lacks, but a philosophy of colors... Blue does not belong to Reckitt’s, but to the sky... The schools must recover and protect [the spirit touching color] if they are really to give the children any imaginative appetite or pleasure in the thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to color is insufficient if it is commercialized or wrongly scaled; art education must teach the significance, scale and motives of color (compare medieval illumination vs. advertising) and cultivate discernment—'turning drunkards into wine tasters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions that know a specific aim succeed (value of focused purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The managers of our public schools did know what sort of boy they liked. They wanted something and they got something... The aristocratic educationists have the positive purpose of turning out gentlemen, and they do turn out gentlemen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts public schools' clear, narrow aims (producing 'gentlemen') with popular schools' vague ambitions (producing citizens) to argue institutional effectiveness arises from having a concrete, pursued ideal—even if that ideal is contested morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and cultivate physical courage (athletics as a fundamental virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Physical courage is a magnificent fundamental... if a man lost that virtue he could never be sure of keeping any other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Athletics and bodily courage are defended as essential foundations for other virtues; Chesterton rejects the view that physical courage necessarily equals cruelty and distinguishes between physical daring and moral viciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate desire for truth rather than partisan game‑playing
rubrics_metrics.description: "No English school-boy is ever taught to tell the truth, for the very simple reason that he is never taught to desire the truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton criticizes public-school debating/play that trains partisanship (taking sides as in sports) rather than inculcating appreciation of factual truth; he ties this failure to broader political culture (the Party System) and urges education to foster a love of veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting conveniences and pleasures into moral virtues (resist hypocrisy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton attacks the 'superstition of soap' and similar tendencies to make pleasures into virtues: e.g., equating physical cleanliness, sport, or forms of charity with moral purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns against moralizing ordinary comforts (soap, sport) and distinguishing between sincere charity and showy, hypocritical attitudes; educators should teach moral understanding of practices rather than treating them as badges of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratize valuable institutions by widening access rather than abolishing them
rubrics_metrics.description: "I do not propose... that we should abolish the public schools. I propose... that we should make them public... make universities fairly universal and property decently proper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than destroy traditional institutions, Chesterton recommends adapting and broadening them (e.g., 'mediaevalize the public schools' to democratize them) so their strengths benefit a wider population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual and ethical education must convey authoritative meaning, not accidental clothing of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: On color and costume: medieval colors were chosen to express meaning (e.g., monk's brown expressing humility) whereas modern dress/colors often express nothing; similarly, ethical education should give material choices meaningful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts intentional symbolic uses of color and dress (heraldry, liturgical vestments) with modern accidental or commercial uses; schools should teach how material culture can communicate moral/aesthetic truths rather than leave it meaningless.
